summary.summary: Haringey's debt is growing fast: loans rose £232.1m during 2025/26 to £1,213.4m at 31 March 2026, funding a large capital programme the council says will continue to be financed largely by new borrowing in coming years. Cash is managed very tight - investment balances swung between £13.6m and £184.3m over the year, with the portfolio's weighted average maturity just 1 day and a year-end return of 3.75%. The Section 151 officer reports full compliance with the Treasury Management Code except lease levels measured against the Operational Boundary and Authorised Limit, an exception first reported at Quarter 3. This is the covering report; the detailed tables (investment position, borrowing detail, indicator-by-indicator compliance) sit in Appendix 1, a separate document.

signals.headline: Loans up £232.1m in 2025/26 to £1,213.4m at 31 March 2026, with the capital programme to be financed largely by new borrowing in upcoming years
signals.why: A 24% one-year jump in debt, with more signalled, raises debt-servicing costs just as short-term LA-to-LA rates spiked to 5-7% at year end.

signals.headline: Investment balances fell as low as £13.6m during 2025/26 (range £13.6m-£184.3m) against a £1.2bn loan book, with portfolio weighted average maturity of 1 day
signals.why: A council of this debt size running an overnight-only cash book with a £13.6m trough depends on continuous access to short-term borrowing markets.

news_drafts.headline: Haringey's 2027-2032 budget gap assumes £84.3m a year of exceptional financial support
news_drafts.lead:
Haringey's forecast budget gap is calculated after assuming "an on-going reliance on EFS of £84.3m" each year, according to the 2027-28 budget and 2027-2032 medium term financial strategy report before cabinet on 10 November. EFS is exceptional financial support, which is permission from government to borrow, or sell assets, to cover day-to-day spending.

The paper says this sum has effectively been built into ongoing budgets and will need to be borrowed each year. It calls this the structural deficit. Permission for EFS must be obtained each year, and any new requirement for 2027/28 will be confirmed later. The report puts the borrowing cost at £86,000 for every £1m borrowed, at 5.85% over 20 years.

The Chartered Institute of Public Finance and Accountancy (CIPFA) has also recently completed a financial review of the council, which is required for councils receiving EFS. The review was commissioned by the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government. The paper states that timescales for publication are not confirmed, and that the council will respond if any recommendations are identified.
news_drafts.paper_title: 1. 2027-28 Budget and 2027-2032 Medium Term Financial Strategy Report

news_drafts.headline: Haringey forecasts £21.7m overspend for 2026/27 after £84.3m of exceptional financial support
news_drafts.lead:
Haringey was forecasting at quarter 1 a full-year overspend of £21.7m for 2026/27, after counting £84.3m of exceptional financial support (EFS), which is government permission to borrow or sell assets to cover day-to-day spending. Without that support the cumulative budget shortfall is £106.0m, according to the council's external auditor in its draft annual report on 2025/26, which goes to the Audit Committee on 3 November.

Full Council approved the £353.0m General Fund budget on 2 March 2026, with an £84.3m gap between planned income and spending. The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government had approved EFS of up to £84.3m on 23 February. For 2025/26 it approved up to £54m, and the final drawdown was £40.6m, against £37m in the approved budget. The paper gives the improved position from quarter 3 to quarter 4 and an unplanned drawdown from earmarked reserves as reasons it was below the ceiling. The auditor says each £1m of EFS adds £83,000 a year to revenue costs for 20 years at current rates, or £8.8m a year on a £106.0m shortfall, assuming principal is repaid at maturity. It also says the speed at which the 2026/27 budget has deteriorated confirms that the budget-setting weakness remains.

The corporate risk register, as at 13 October 2026, keeps reducing reliance on EFS as Risk 1, at the highest level, scored 25 now and 20 in future. It records reliance rising from at least £37m in 2025/26 to £84m in 2026/27. Its actions include a revised Financial Sustainability Plan, from the chief executive and section 151 officer, aimed at balancing the budget in year across the next three years, and external independence added to the Finance Recovery Board. The register states that none of the actions is yet completed or fully embedded.

news_drafts.headline: Haringey pension fund paid £74.5m in benefits in 2025/26 against £67.8m received in contributions
news_drafts.lead:
Haringey's pension fund paid out £74.5m in benefits in 2025/26 and received £67.8m in contributions, a difference of £6.7m. The figures are in the fund's draft annual report for the year, which was among the papers for the council's Pensions Committee and Board on 15 October 2026.

The report says the £6.7m was covered by investment income in the year. It also says benefits have exceeded contributions for several years. In its words: "Contributions have grown at a slower pace than benefits paid, reflecting the increasing maturity of the Fund's membership profile."

The report describes active membership as declining relative to the number of pensioners and deferred members, meaning people who have left the scheme but not yet drawn their pension. The annual report is in draft.

findings.headline: Forecast price inflation adds £4,067k across 2027/28 to 2031/32, described in the paper as an average of 15%.
findings.detail: Corporate Budgets adjusts pay inflation at 3.5% in 2027/28 and 3% from 2028/29 onwards, netting to £2,145k across the period. The price inflation line totals £4,067k, with £1,945k in 2031/32 alone.
findings.matters: The inflation assumptions drive the corporate budget lines in this table, and the stated 15% average for price inflation is a specific assumption other councils' finance officers can compare against their own.
findings.quote: Total increase for forecast Price Inflation

findings.headline: Resident Support Service is to need additional funding from 2027/28, with the amount not yet set.
findings.detail: The paper says the service has had large cost savings in the past without the digital infrastructure needed to move customers online, and that it will need additional funding in 2027/28. The precise requirement is being developed and will be set out in the February budget papers.
findings.matters: This is a service pressure the council has not yet costed, and a finance director or lender will want to see the figure when it appears in the February budget papers.
findings.quote: The precise requirement is being developed and will be set out in the February budget papers.

findings.headline: Loss of income from a Government £100 cap on court costs is £300k in 2027/28.
findings.detail: Environment & Resident Experience records a £300k income loss in 2027/28 from the Government's cap on court costs introduced at £100. The same line carries a bracketed note reading '(loss of £32)' that the paper does not explain.
findings.matters: A national cap on court cost recovery changes income for any council that recovers those costs, so peer finance officers will want to see the size of the effect here.
findings.quote: Loss of income from Government cap introduced at £100 for court costs

findings.headline: Corporate Budgets show (£3,000k) in 2027/28 from removing an assumed Budget Planning Reserve replenishment and reversing a 2025/26 Collection Fund Smoothing reserve drawdown.
findings.detail: This is a single entry in 2027/28 with no later-year figures. The paper treats the Budget Planning Reserve replenishment as assumed and reverses the 2025/26 drawdown from the Collection Fund Smoothing reserve.
findings.matters: Reserve replenishments and drawdowns show how far the budget depends on reserves between years, which lenders and peer finance officers check when assessing a council's financial resilience.
findings.quote: Removal of Assumed replenishment of Budget Planning Reserve

findings.headline: Housing Benefit subsidy loss linked to Temporary Accommodation rents is £7,780k over 2027/28 to 2029/30, of which £7,741k falls in 2027/28.
findings.detail: The paper attributes the subsidy loss to higher Temporary Accommodation rents, stating that the Department for Work and Pensions does not reimburse the full TA rent charged and that higher rents generate both additional income and additional subsidy costs. Housing Demand totals £11,458k, including £2,410k for increase in demand and price of temporary accommodation.
findings.matters: The paper shows a cost that rises with the council's own TA rent income, so the gross income gain is paired with a subsidy cost, a relationship councils with similar DWP subsidy gaps will recognise.
findings.figures: £7,741k (2027/28); £19k (2028/29); £20k (2029/30); £7,780k total subsidy loss; £11,458k Housing Demand total; £2,410k TA demand and price
findings.quote: The Department for Work and Pensions does not reimburse the full Temporary Accommodation rent charged by the Council.

daily_post.headline: The Financial Recovery Silver and Gold Groups were replaced by a Financial Recovery Board during 2025/26.
daily_post.lead: A change in the body that oversees financial recovery is a governance change that other councils with recovery plans may recognise and compare.
